items.followUp: Describe how the cell plate develops into a new cell wall during plant-cell cytokinesis.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the material and place where the cell plate begins to form.
rubric.description: Golgi vesicles gather at the equator and fuse.
rubric.how: Look for vesicles (or Golgi vesicles) accumulating or joining at the cell’s equator to form the plate; accept equivalent wording involving vesicles from the Golgi apparatus coming together there.

rubric.why: Award for describing how the plate grows and separates the daughter cells.
rubric.description: The cell plate grows outward and develops into a separating cell wall.
rubric.how: Look for growth of the plate towards the cell edges and/or its development into a new wall dividing the daughter cells.

modelAnswer: Golgi vesicles gather and fuse at the equator of the dividing plant cell to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outward and develops into a new cell wall, separating the daughter cells.

items.followUp: How do homologous chromosome pairs arrange themselves during metaphase I of meiosis?

rubric.why: Award for identifying what lines up and where it lines up.
rubric.description: Homologous chromosome pairs (bivalents) arrange at the cell equator.
rubric.how: Look for homologous pairs or bivalents positioned along the equatorial plane.

rubric.why: Award for describing the spindle attachment associated with the metaphase arrangement.
rubric.description: Spindle fibres attach to the chromosomes from opposite poles.
rubric.how: Look for spindle fibres attaching to the chromosomes or their centromeres, with fibres extending from opposite poles.

modelAnswer: Homologous chromosome pairs (bivalents) arrange themselves along the equatorial plane, forming the metaphase plate.
Spindle fibres from opposite poles attach to the chromosomes.

items.followUp: Compare the light-dependent and light-independent stages of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Award for a correct feature of the light reaction.
rubric.description: The light reaction takes place in the thylakoids (grana) and requires light.
rubric.how: Look for the light requirement and/or its location in the thylakoids or grana.

rubric.why: Award for a correct contrast describing the dark reaction.
rubric.description: The dark reaction occurs in the stroma and uses carbon dioxide and products of the light reaction to make carbohydrates.
rubric.how: Look for its location in the stroma and/or the use of carbon dioxide with ATP and NADPH to form carbohydrates; accept that it does not directly require light.

modelAnswer: The light reaction occurs in the thylakoids (grana), requires light, and produces ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
The dark reaction occurs in the stroma; it uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and does not directly require light.

items.followUp: Name the main products of glycolysis and state its net ATP yield.

rubric.why: Award for the main carbon-containing product of glycolysis.
rubric.description: Glycolysis produces two molecules of pyruvate (pyruvic acid).
rubric.how: Look for the yield of two pyruvate or pyruvic acid molecules.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the energy products of glycolysis.
rubric.description: Glycolysis yields a net two ATP and also produces two NADH.
rubric.how: Look for a net yield of two ATP; NADH may also be named.

modelAnswer: One glucose molecule produces two molecules of pyruvic acid (pyruvate) in glycolysis.
The net yield is two ATP molecules; two NADH molecules are also produced.

items.followUp: Explain how enzymes increase the rate of biochemical reactions.

rubric.why: Award for stating the mechanism by which enzymes speed reactions.
rubric.description: Enzymes lower the activation energy of reactions.
rubric.how: Look for the idea that enzymes reduce or lower the activation energy needed for a reaction.

rubric.why: Award for explaining the effect or reusable nature of enzymes.
rubric.description: This makes reactions faster; enzymes are not used up in the reactions.
rubric.how: Look for a statement that reactions proceed faster and/or that enzymes remain unchanged and can be reused.

modelAnswer: Enzymes lower the activation energy required for biological reactions.
This makes the reactions occur faster, while the enzymes remain unchanged and can be reused.

items.followUp: Give two examples of enzymes used in food processing and state what each is used for.

rubric.why: Award for one correct enzyme and its food-industry use.
rubric.description: One valid enzyme application is identified.
rubric.how: Look for a correct enzyme-use pair, such as amylase in bread making, rennin in cheese making, protease for meat tenderising, or pectinase in juice processing.

rubric.why: Award for a second valid enzyme application.
rubric.description: A second valid enzyme application is identified.
rubric.how: Look for another correct enzyme-use pair; it must be different from the example credited for the first mark.

modelAnswer: Amylase is used in bread making.
Rennin (rennet) is used in cheese making.

items.followUp: What causes a heart attack, and why does it damage heart muscle?

rubric.why: Award for identifying the blocked blood supply that causes the condition.
rubric.description: A coronary artery becomes blocked or obstructed.
rubric.how: Look for blockage or obstruction of a coronary artery, or an equivalent statement that blood supply to the heart muscle is cut off.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the resulting damage to the heart muscle.
rubric.description: The affected heart muscle is deprived of oxygen and is damaged or dies.
rubric.how: Look for oxygen deprivation and damage or death of heart muscle; accepting “heart attack” as a synonym requires the cause or effect to be stated as well for this mark.

modelAnswer: Myocardial infarction, or a heart attack, occurs when a coronary artery is blocked.
The affected heart muscle receives too little oxygen, causing some of its tissue to become damaged or die.

items.followUp: State two ways in which transpiration is important to a plant.

rubric.why: Award for a role in moving water or minerals through the plant.
rubric.description: Transpiration helps move water and mineral salts from roots towards the leaves.
rubric.how: Look for ascent of sap or transport of water and minerals from roots to leaves.

rubric.why: Award for another valid importance of transpiration.
rubric.description: Transpiration cools the plant and/or helps maintain cell turgidity.
rubric.how: Look for cooling or maintenance of turgidity; do not award this mark for merely repeating water or mineral transport.

modelAnswer: Transpiration helps in the upward transport of water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves (ascent of sap).
It also cools the plant and helps maintain cell turgidity.
